title: Instance-Optimal Estimation with Multiple LLM Judges on a Budget
claim: Our adaptive estimator tracks the oracle allocation and clearly beats uniform allocation across budgets, on synthetic and real data.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared legend style, shaded quantile bands
description: Two side-by-side line plots show L2 error against budget. Panel (a) is synthetic data with K=1000 and J=10, and the budget runs from 1e7 to 9e7. Panel (b) is the real 'Complexity' dataset with K=178 and J=3, and the budget runs from 0.2e3 to 5e3. Each panel has four curves. Uniform is a grey dashed line with circles. Oracle is blue with squares. Est-IVWE (Bounded) is red with triangles. Est-IVWE (Gaussian) is green with diamonds. Shaded bands show the 10–90% quantiles over 50 runs. In (a), uniform sits well above the others. The Est-IVWE curves converge toward the oracle as budget grows. In (b), the Est-IVWE curves start high at small budgets, with wide bands, and then drop to near the oracle. Uniform plateaus higher. Panel captions sit below the plots.
caption: Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets. All results are averaged over $50$ independent runs, with the $10%$ and $90%$ quantiles (shaded regions)
abstract: Evaluating large language models increasingly relies on LLM-as-a-judge protocols, but such evaluations remain costly: different judges have different prices and reliabilities, and the difficulty of each prompt-response pair can vary substantially. This raises a basic allocation question: under a fixed budget, how should one distribute evaluation queries across heterogeneous judges and instances to obtain the most accurate score estimates? We formalize this question as budgeted heteroskedastic multi-judge estimation under independent, unbiased score observations. Given $K$ prompt-response pairs and $J$ judges with known costs but unknown query-judge variances, our goal is to estimate the bounded score vector while minimizing an $\ell_p$-error. Our first contribution is to analyze the inverse-variance weighted estimator (IVWE) and to derive the oracle allocation that minimizes its leading error bound. Since this allocation depends on the unknown variances, we then address the unknown-variance setting by proposing EST-IVWE, an adaptive algorithm that constructs and uses optimistic variance estimates to stabilize the empirical allocation. We prove that EST-IVWE matches the oracle IVWE rate up to lower-order terms in the budget. Our second and central theoretical contribution is a local minimax lower bound matching the leading allocation-dependent rate, establishing asymptotic instance-optimality up to logarithmic factors. An Assouad-type construction based on local, variance-preserving perturbations yields this bound both in expectation and with constant probability. A complementary Fano-type change-of-measure argument captures the logarithmic dependence on the confidence level with a different (suboptimal) allocation geometry. Finally, we numerically validate our approach on synthetic data and resampled HelpSteer2 evaluations, demonstrating improvements over naÃ¯ve uniform allocation.
